label: Start Here
title: Philosophy Foundations: What You Need Before Page One
tagline: A gentle toolkit for reading arguments about God, no philosophy class required
oneSentence: Before you open Feser’s *Five Proofs*, you need a small toolkit — how arguments work, what makes one a “demonstration,” the Aristotelian ideas of act and potency, form and matter, essence and existence, the difference between a chain of causes stretching back in time and a stack of causes operating right now, and what classical theists actually mean by “God” — and this module teaches every one of those tools slowly, with everyday examples.
bigPicture:
Edward Feser’s *Five Proofs of the Existence of God* (2017) is written so that a non-philosopher can follow it, but it still moves fast. Each chapter starts “in the shallow end,” as Feser puts it, and ends in the deepest part of the pool. Readers who have never studied philosophy usually get lost not because the arguments are too hard, but because a handful of background ideas are introduced quickly and then used on every page afterward: **potentiality and actuality**, **hierarchical causal series**, **essence and existence**, the **principle of sufficient reason**, **universals**, **simplicity**, and the **analogical** use of words. Miss one of these and the next forty pages feel like fog.

This module is the fog-lifter. It does not argue for God’s existence — that is the book’s job. It gives you the vocabulary and the habits of mind the book assumes: how to find the premises and conclusion in a paragraph, how deduction differs from induction and from “inference to the best explanation,” what it means for an argument to be *valid* versus *sound*, how to recognize the fallacies Feser keeps pointing to (the fallacy of composition, begging the question, the straw man, special pleading, the god of the gaps), and how to talk about what is *necessary*, *contingent*, and *possible*.

Then it hands you Aristotle’s toolkit — substance and accident, form and matter, the four causes, act and potency — and spends extra time on the single most important idea in the book: the difference between a **linear (per accidens)** series of causes, like a line of ancestors, and a **hierarchical (per se)** series, like a cup held up by a desk held up by a floor, *right now*. Almost every famous objection to Feser’s arguments (“Who made God?”, “Why can’t the regress be infinite?”, “Maybe the universe had no beginning”) turns on missing this distinction.

Finally, the module explains what Feser means by “God.” He defends **classical theism**: God is not a very powerful being inside the universe but pure actuality, absolutely simple, unchanging, timeless, the source of the existence of everything else. Many debates about God go nowhere because the two sides are talking about different things. You will finish this module knowing exactly what the book is trying to prove, how its chapters are built, and how to read a 50-step formal argument without panic.
objectives: Define natural theology and explain how it differs from revealed theology (faith in what God has revealed) and from empirical science.
Identify the premises, conclusion, and hidden premises of an argument written in ordinary prose, using indicator words.
Distinguish deduction, induction, and inference to the best explanation, and explain why Feser claims his proofs are demonstrations rather than probable hypotheses.
Explain the difference between a valid and a sound argument, and state the two legitimate ways to attack a deductive argument.
Recognize and give an everyday example of the fallacy of composition, begging the question, the straw man, special pleading, ad hominem, and the god-of-the-gaps move.
Explain actuality and potentiality with three examples, and use them to state the principle of causality in Feser’s precise form.
Distinguish a linear (per accidens) causal series from a hierarchical (per se) causal series, and explain why only the second must have a first member — and what “first” means there.
Explain the real distinction between essence and existence, the principle of sufficient reason, and the realist, nominalist, and conceptualist views of universals.
Contrast classical theism with theistic personalism, and explain how univocal, equivocal, and analogical language differ when we call God “good” or “wise.”

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
This is the very first stop in the course, and it is designed for someone who has never taken a philosophy class. You do not need to believe in God, disbelieve in God, or know anything about Aristotle to begin. You only need curiosity and a willingness to go slowly.

**What this module is for.** Feser’s book defends five arguments that God exists. Each argument uses a few specialized tools — words like *potentiality*, *essence*, *contingent*, *hierarchical series*. Feser explains them as he goes, but quickly. This module teaches those tools in advance, one at a time, with ordinary examples (coffee cooling, a cup on a desk, a $20 bill), so that when you meet them in the book they feel like old friends.

**How to use the whole course.** Every module follows the same rhythm, and it works best in this order:

1. **Preview** the module here: read the plain-English box at the top of each lesson, then the full lesson, then try the quick checks.
2. **Watch** the module’s video (made in NotebookLM from the module’s study document) for a relaxed overview.
3. **Read** the chapter in the book, using the reading map for that module to know where to slow down.
4. **Return** to the module for practice: the argument walk-through, objections, quiz, flashcards, and the teach-back challenge.

This primer is the one exception: there is no book chapter to read afterward. Instead, when you finish it you will read Feser’s short Introduction (pages 9–15) and then chapter 1.

**What you will be asked to accept.** Nothing, yet. This module explains ideas; it does not require you to agree with them. You will learn how Feser uses words, why he thinks his arguments are more than guesses, and what he means by “God.” Whether his arguments succeed is something you will judge for yourself chapter by chapter.

**Reassurance about the hard parts.** Two lessons carry most of the weight: lesson 7 (act and potency) and lesson 8 (hierarchical versus linear causal series). If they feel slippery, that is normal — philosophers took centuries to state them carefully. Read them twice, try the examples with objects on your own desk, and do not move on until you can explain the cup–desk–floor example out loud. Everything else in the book gets easier once those two ideas click.

knowFirst.plain: A set of reasons (premises) offered to support a claim (the conclusion). In philosophy an argument is not a quarrel; it is a chain of reasoning you can inspect link by link.

An argument is valid when its conclusion really follows: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. Validity is about the shape of the reasoning, not whether the premises are actually true.
A deductive argument whose conclusion follows necessarily from premises that are certain. This is what Feser claims his proofs are — not ‘probably God,’ but ‘God, necessarily, given these premises.’
Something that exists but could have failed to exist, like you, a tree, or the moon. The opposite of necessary.
A real capacity a thing has but is not using yet: hot coffee can become cold; it cannot become chicken soup. Aristotle’s word for ‘what a thing can be.’
The way a thing actually is right now: the coffee’s actual heat, your actual reading of this sentence. Only something actual can make a potential become actual.

A chain of causes where every link works only because the link above it is working at the same time — a cup held up by a desk, held up by a floor, held up by the earth. This kind of chain must have a first member with power of its own.
What a thing is — its nature, what makes it the kind of thing it is (a triangle is a closed three-sided figure). Different from the fact that it exists.
The principle that everything has an explanation — either in itself or in something else. Nothing is simply there for no reason at all.
The traditional view of God defended in the book: not a big being in the universe but pure actuality — simple, unchanging, timeless, the source of the existence of everything else.

questionsToHold: When Feser says he has a “proof,” what exactly is he claiming — certainty, high probability, or something else? What would count as refuting it?
Is a potential “nothing,” or is it a real feature of things? What would follow if it were nothing at all?
When I ask what caused something, am I asking about its past (what got it started) or its present (what keeps it going right now)?
Could a chain of things that each have only borrowed power explain anything, however long the chain is?
Does the word “God” in this debate mean the same thing to believers and skeptics? What would each side need to agree on before arguing?
Can a word like “good” or “cause” mean something true of God without meaning exactly what it means of a person or a machine?

map.what: Feser explains what natural theology is, why this is not a commentary on Aquinas’ Five Ways, how every proof chapter is built (informal Stage 1, informal Stage 2, formal statement, objections), previews all seven chapters, and makes the bold claim that the proofs succeed and that the real debate is among different kinds of theists.
map.tip: Read it in one sitting right after finishing this primer. Underline the definition of natural theology and the two-stage description of each proof; you will use both constantly.

map.what: From the fact of change to a purely actual actualizer (the Unmoved Mover). Introduces act and potency, the principle of causality, linear versus hierarchical series, and derives the divine attributes. Then a 50-step formal statement and long objection sections (Hume, Kant, Russell, Newton, Einstein, quantum mechanics).
map.tip: Pages 17–29 are the heart of the whole book: go slowly and reread the cup–desk–floor pages (21–26). The science-based objections (pages 43–63) can be skimmed on a first read and revisited later.

map.what: Things made of parts need something to hold their parts together here and now; the regress ends in something absolutely simple, Plotinus’ “the One.” Introduces metaphysical parts (form and matter, essence and existence) and the analogical use of language.
map.tip: Short and elegant. Slow down where Feser explains how many divine attributes can belong to one simple reality — lesson 12 of this primer prepares you for it.

map.what: Universals, propositions, numbers, and possible worlds are real but are neither physical things nor mere human ideas; the only adequate ground for them is an eternal divine intellect. Covers realism, nominalism, conceptualism, and three kinds of realism.
map.tip: Review lesson 11 first. The six arguments for realism (pages 90–92) are worth outlining in your notes; the later objections (Leftow, Grim) can be read lightly the first time.

map.what: In every ordinary thing, what it is (essence) is really distinct from the fact that it is (existence); such things need a cause that conjoins their essence and existence at every moment, ending in something whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself.
map.tip: Master the three arguments for the real distinction (pages 117–122) before going on. Kenny’s objection (pages 135–141) is the most technical passage; read it last.

map.what: Defends the principle of sufficient reason and argues that contingent things can only be ultimately explained by a necessary being whose existence is explained by its own nature. Discusses brute facts, infinite series, and the fallacy of composition.
map.tip: Very readable. Pay close attention to why PSR is not the same as the principle of causality (page 148) and to the geometry-book example (pages 155–157).

map.section: Chapter 6: The Nature of God and of His Relationship to the World
map.what: The longest chapter: three background principles (proportionate causality, agere sequitur esse, analogy), then God’s unity, simplicity, immutability, eternity, necessity, omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility; then conservation, concurrence, and miracles. In this course it is split into two modules (6A: pages 169–205; 6B: pages 205–248).
map.tip: Do not read it in one go. Lessons 13 and 14 of this primer (classical theism, analogy) are your preparation. Take a break after the section on eternity and necessity (around page 208).

map.section: Chapter 7: Common Objections to Natural Theology
map.what: Answers the popular objections: “What caused God?”, the straw-man “basic cosmological argument,” infinite regress, the fallacy of composition, god of the gaps, scientism, “one god further,” the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, and whether something controversial can be a proof. Split in this course into 7A (pages 249–273) and 7B (pages 273–308).
map.tip: The most conversational chapter and very useful for real discussions. The section on scientism (pages 273–286) repays careful study; the evil and hiddenness sections should be read slowly and with patience.

afterReading: Without looking, explain the difference between a potential and an actuality using an example from your own kitchen.
Draw the cup–desk–floor–earth stack and the grandfather–father–son line side by side, and explain in two sentences why only the stack needs a first member.
State the principle of causality in Feser’s exact form (not “everything has a cause”) and explain why that difference defuses “Who made God?”
Take a short opinion article and mark its conclusion, its premises, one hidden premise, and any indicator words.
Explain to an imaginary friend why a demonstration is attacked differently from a scientific hypothesis.
List four attributes of God in classical theism and explain why a “very powerful being inside the universe” would not have them.
Explain what the word “good” means in “good wine” and “good man,” and why that is analogy rather than equivocation.
If you can do all of the above, you are ready for the Introduction (pages 9–15) and chapter 1.
